title: Japan’s October policy debate turns on how quickly to approach neutral
summary: The opinions submitted after the Bank of Japan’s 29–30 October meeting reveal a dispute about how much accommodation remained. Several contributions favoured maintaining the policy rate at that meeting while the effects of previous increases worked through the economy. Other submissions argued for an earlier return to neutral now that underlying inflation appeared consistent with the 2% target. The difference matters for the path of short rates. An economy able to absorb previous hikes with little effect could need more tightening, but the same absence of an immediate slowdown could mean the effect was still to come. This publication, issued on 10 November, gives edited, unattributed contributions from members and government representatives. Its bullets cannot be counted as votes (p. 1, footnote 2; section II, pp. 3–5).

The economic account contained a similar distinction between resilience and momentum. Higher energy and material costs were expected to slow fiscal 2026 growth, with government measures and global AI demand helping Japan continue to expand. One assessment expected a moderate pickup from fiscal 2027 as the cost shock faded. Another emphasised the concentration of the AI impulse in semiconductor inputs, equipment and data centres. Employment and income could support household spending without consumption leading the recovery. The average Consumption Activity Index for July and August had fallen relative to the April–June quarter. One contribution interpreted the international links more broadly, arguing that Japan had become more exposed to ordinary global business cycles following its long period of deflation (section I, pp. 1–2).

The inflation disagreement centred on persistence. Labour shortages and firms’ willingness to raise pay supported the view that wages and prices could continue rising at a pace consistent with target. Some employers expected next year’s increases to resemble this year’s. Another contribution saw little reason for wage growth to accelerate and limited evidence that recent oil-price increases had produced second-round effects. Government measures lowering consumer prices might also influence wage bargaining. One submission projected annual CPI inflation excluding fresh food above 3% towards the fiscal year-end. That projection concerned a measured price index; it does not establish that the underlying rate would reach 3%. The spring wage negotiations, actual price outcomes and inflation expectations were proposed as ways to assess whether underlying inflation would stay near 2% (pp. 2–3).

The disagreement extends to measuring the stance. One contribution proposed examining the real interest rate relative to neutral, corporate finance and bank lending, and asset prices. In particular, a stock-market rise led by global AI demand gave ambiguous evidence about Japanese monetary policy. One view put neutral considerably above 1%; another judged that the policy rate had already entered its estimated range. Those assessments have different implications for the next increase. Some saw an early move towards neutral as a way to regain room to respond in either direction. Others wanted to observe financial conditions for several months after each increase, or expected inflation to settle near target with gradual hikes. A further increase could also restrain already supply-constrained housing and business investment (pp. 3–5).

A separate discussion concerned disposals of the Bank’s exchange-traded funds. Sales had been running since January. Submissions pointed to their orderly execution and greater stock-market turnover as grounds to reconsider the pace, while also raising the governance implications of central-bank equity ownership. The views specify no revised sale volume. The Finance Ministry and Cabinet Office expected the Bank to exercise its judgement on disposals; their remarks are identified separately from members’ monetary policy assessments. The document gives no priced probability for the next rate move or market reaction to a change in sales (pp. 5–6).

questions.question: Which evidence would separate a genuinely high neutral rate from delayed restraint?
questions.detail: The opinions support both readings of resilient corporate activity. Their implications for Japanese front-end rates diverge after a further increase. Compare scheduled repricing on existing bank loans with new borrowing rates, investment plans and loan volumes across firms with different refinancing dates. The Bank’s lending statistics and business surveys, alongside borrower disclosures, could show whether higher costs have reached firms already or remain ahead.

questions.question: What would count as a second round from oil into wages?
questions.detail: The submissions identify wage bargaining as informative and acknowledge that government measures could affect the prices workers observe. Compare the spring pay proposals and settlements with wage-sensitive services prices and firms’ intentions to raise selling prices. Official wage statistics, union releases and the Bank’s enterprise surveys could distinguish compensation for one earlier price-level increase from repeated wage and price revisions that would change the pace of tightening.

questions.question: Could larger ETF sales be absorbed on less liquid days?
questions.detail: The experience cited concerns the sales pace already attempted while turnover was expanding. For equity-market exposure, average turnover gives an incomplete measure of the risk from larger disposals during weak trading. Seek the Bank’s disposal rules and published execution totals, and compare the prospective sale size with turnover across ordinary and stressed sessions. This would test market capacity without reading a particular sale target into the opinions.
